newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian housing upturn seen intact despite fall.
newsitem.headline: Australian housing upturn seen intact despite fall.

text.p: Australia's housing sector remains in modest upturn and is positioned to strengthen modestly during 1997, despite news of a larger than expected fall in housing finance approvals during May, economists said.

The housing finance series has been more volatile than usual over the past three months, with seasonal adjustment factors unable to adequately compensate for the earlier than usual occurrence of Easter this year.
Housing finance approvals fell by 8.4 percent in May, official figures released on Friday showed.
While this was larger than the 5.7 percent decline expected by economists, it did not reverse April's 12.2 percent rise, and left the trend for the series on a moderate incline.
"The seasonally adjusted housing finance data continues to saw-tooth, but the trend suggests sustained strength," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary.
Much of this decline was due to a large drop in the refinancing of existing loans, which was down 22.6 percent in the month.
Finance approvals excluding refinancing fell 3.9 percent.
More importantly for the building industry, approvals for construction and new lending showed some resilience in the month.
Approvals for construction and new lending fell by 2.4 percent in the month, after rising by 15.3 percent in April.
As a percentage of total loans, they rose to 20.4 percent, the first time they have been above 20 percent of total loans since mid 1995.
"Finance for new construction and for newly erected dwellings remains firm suggesting continued improvement in dwelling construction over 1997," HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said.

This sector is seen as important for the flow through effects to other areas of the economy as it is growth in new housing that will lead to increased employment, and increased demand for housing materials and consumer goods.

However, the data showed that while housing was in upturn, it was not as strong as previous upturns had been, nor that the upturn would be as strong as the data was indicating in the second half of 1996.

"This conclusion, that the indications are for a modest housing upturn, is consistent with signals coming from a range of housing data, including building approvals, and suggests there is little risk at present of an excessive housing boom emerging in the foreseeable future, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Tony Meer said.

Given the ongoing expectations of a housing upturn, and allowing for the fact that the May 23 cut in official interest rates would not have had any impact on the month's data, economists said the data had little impact on the monetary policy outlook.
If anything, the housing sector upturn was an argument against a cut, but this was outweighed by weakness in other areas such as employment and the manufacturing sector.
